reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
In this manuscript, Zhong et al. present the structures of human V1aR in its apo state and in complexes with different
antagonists. Overall, the manuscript is well-written. I am not a structural biologist and so am only commenting on the single
molecule photobleaching experiment in Figure 2 b-f which I believe needs additional clarification and replicates to
demonstrate statistical robustness.
Briefly - the authors perform single molecule photobleaching experiments in fixed cells that are transiently expressing GFP-
tagged versions of the WT and K52A/A59Y versions of their protein. They conclude that the WT protein shows
predominantly two-step photobleaching whereas the mutant protein shows single step photobleaching. Below are
comments and suggestions for improvement:
Major Comments:
1) The authors describe a need to maintain “very-low” expression levels to minimize overexpression artifacts, yet it does not
appear that they actually quantify the expression levels in cells. How do the fluorescently tagged protein levels compare to
endogeneous levels in WT cells?
2) It would be helpful if the authors could confirm that the GFP-tagged constructs are still functionally active. E.G. do cells
expressing the GFP-tagged constructs respond similarly to agonism/antagonism compared to the non-fluorescently tagged
proteins?
3) The authors show a representative image in Figure 2c, but do not state what the cell in the image is expressing.
Furthermore, they indicate that only spots within the yellow circles were chosen for further analysis, but they do not state how
these spots were selected or why they were chosen instead of the many other puncta-like objects in their image. I’m also
concerned that the representative image shows many large aggregates of protein in addition to single diffraction-limited
spots. What are these large aggregate structures? Are they an oligomerization artifact due to the tagged protein?
4) There are no error bars on Figure 2 e or f, nor do the authors provide information about the sample size (number of spots,
number of cells, nor number biological replicates). Are these plots from just a single ROI in a single cell each?
5) At least in my experience, it is very unusual to have single molecule photobleaching defined by only monomers or dimers
and not have any higher-order oligomerization states (even if only at a small percentage). Were these curves discarded from
the analysis?
6) There is no information in the methods about how the number of bleaching steps for each trajectory was determined. Was
this just done manually from the traces or did the authors utilize some objective criteria or algorithm?

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Point-by-point response to reviewers’ comments
We sincerely appreciate the time and expertise dedicated by all the reviewers whose constructive
comments have significantly strengthened our work. In response, we have carefully addressed all
points raised using additional experiments and have revised the manuscript to incorporate the
suggestions. All changes have been incorporated and are highlighted in the revised submission.
Below is a point-by-point response to the reviewers (our response is in blue):
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
[...]
Reply: Thank you for your suggestion. For the apo-state, we collected more images (from 4860
images to 8642 images now), which increases the final particles from 319,985 to 504,370. The
overall resolution of the cryo-EM map has been improved from 2.9 Å to 2.8 Å. While the
improvement in global resolution is modest, the local map quality has been significantly
enhanced.
Using the new map of the apo state, the majority of ECL2 was reliably modeled, supported by
well-defined local densities (please refer to Fig. 3b for local densities and Supplementary Fig.
6c for the exact protein sequence included in the final model). The model of the apo-state
actually includes the protein segments of ECL2 that form the antiparallel beta-sheet observed in
the antagonist-bound states (Supplementary Fig. 6c). Interestingly, in the apo structure, these
regions adopt alpha-helical conformations: one becomes a continuation of TM4, while the other
inserts into the ligand-binding pocket (Fig. 3a, b, Supplementary Fig. 6c). The two cysteines
(one in TM3, and the other in ECL2) that form a disulfide bond in the antagonist bound states are
both clearly resolved in the cryo-EM density in the apo form (Fig. 3b). They are spatially
separated, with bulky residues such as F207 and W111 positioned between them (Fig. 3b). This
arrangement provides strong structural evidence that the two cysteines remain unpaired in the
apo state.
The region of ECL2 missing in the apo-state structure (residues 193-201; improved compared to
the previous version) is not part of the antiparallel beta-sheet, but the flexible loop connecting the
two beta-sheet segments. This region in the apo-state is visible as continuous and complete
densities in the 6Å low-pass-filtered map (Supplementary Fig. 5f; the map has been uploaded
for your evaluation). However, due to the limited resolution in this region, reliable atomic
modeling is difficult, and thus, this segment was not included in the final model. Nevertheless,
the absence of this region in the final model does not affect our conclusion that ECL2 in the apo-
state adopts a planar orientation relative to the membrane in the apo structure, and thus is
designated as the “flat” conformation.
Indeed, the majority of disulfide bonds are formed in the ER. However, the oxidative
extracellular environment, along with cell surface protein disulfide isomerase, can also facilitate
disulfide bond formation or rearrangement, as demonstrated in studies (PMID: 22653978). In the
case of GPCRs, a recent study on GPR4 (PMID: 39753131) demonstrated that ECL2 in the apo
state has unpaired cysteines. We speculate that this apo state is a ground state. The transition
from alpha-helical to beta-sheet could be very dynamic, which allows the selective recognition of
the right ligand, while minimizing nonspecific interactions, particularly because the ligand-
binding cavity in the “up” conformation is exceptionally large and exposed.
We modified Fig. 3b, c, made new Supplementary Fig. 6c/Supplementary Fig. 5f, and
modified text (lines 265-276, lines 282-284) to accommodate the new changes.
2/ minor criticisms:
a) If we look at the density map of the apo state, there is a density on the intracellular side at the
dimer interface between TM1 and TM7 which has not been assigned. This density is present in
the two copies of the V1aR, symmetrically. Would this density correspond to a phospholipid? To
a cholesterol molecule? Could this density correspond to part of helix 8 which is actually not
seen?
Reply: Thank you for your question. We also noticed this density on the intracellular side. Based
on the shape and size, we think it might be cholesterol (Please see the figure below for fitting).
To be more conservative on the modeling building, we keep it unassigned.
b) Again, in the apo state structure, if we overlap the density and the corresponding three-
dimensional model at the level of the extracellular loop 3 (ECL3), it is quite difficult to fit the
residues in the density. I think some residues of the ECL3 should be removed.
Reply: Thank you for your suggestion. We reexamined the ECL3 density in the new map of the
apo state and removed residue 325 from the final model.
c) All the structures solved in this study are those of dimeric V1aR. Indeed, size-exclusion
chromatography (supplementary figure 1) and SDS-PAGE of the cryo-EM samples show
purified dimeric species, in agreement with the homodimers seen in live cells. However,
monomeric species are also seen in the samples that were pooled for subsequent cryo-EM grid
preparations. I understand that image processing was started with an initial set of particles from
which the software was trained to define those particles as templates containing only dimers,
before picking the complete set of particles across all micrographs. Do the authors also see
monomer particles in their cryo-EM preparations and micrographs? Would it be possible to
process these particles like dimer particles, keeping in mind the size of these particles is perhaps
too small for a single particle cryo-EM approach?
Reply: Thank you for your question. We also observed a small population of particles with a
smaller diameter in raw images, likely corresponding to the monomeric species. We have tried to
use different templates as well as particle diameter settings to select as many particles as possible
during particle picking. However, due to their small size and low abundance, these particles were
very likely lost during subsequent data processing and do not generate a reliable 3D
reconstruction.
We modified the text (lines 192-195) to accommodate the new changes.
d) In absence of the nanobody 1 (Nb1), the resolution of the maps was very limited, whereas in
the presence of Nb1, the overall resolution of the four maps is high (between 2.6 and 3
angstroms). Thus, the presence of Nb1 certainly stabilizes the complexes. Although Nb1
facilitated particle classification and alignment, its density was not resolved in the final maps.
The authors suggest that Nb1 binds to a relatively flexible part of V1aR. Based on the stability of
the complexes, is this conclusion not paradoxical?
Reply: Thank you for your question, and we apologize for any confusion. The limited resolution
in the absence of Nb1 primarily arises from the lack of a sufficient fiducial mask outside the
detergent micelle to guide particle alignment, which is a very common issue in cryo-EM studies
of apo GPCRs. Although Nb1 is not well resolved in the final high-resolution reconstructions,
the 6Å low–pass–filtered map reveals extra densities adjacent to the cytosolic face of V1aR that
closely match the shape of Nb1 (Supplementary Fig. 5e). This indicates that Nb1 binds to a
conformationally heterogeneous epitope on the intracellular side of the receptor. This binding
position is also far away from the dimer interface, making it unlikely that Nb1 stabilizes the
complexes.
We therefore infer that Nb1 here primarily serves as a fiducial mask, facilitating early particle
classifications and global low-resolution alignment. However, its flexible orientation relative to
the receptor leads to partial signal averaging and eventual loss of nanobody density during high-
resolution refinement.
We made a new Supplementary Fig. 5e and modified the text (lines 169-176) to explain this
better.
e) To my opinion, the comparison of the different antagonist-bound V1aR structures is very
interesting and is not sufficiently discussed. In supplementary figure 6, the structure of V1aR
bound by atosiban, balovaptan and SRX246 were superimposed, but only the receptor is shown.
Once the three structures are aligned based on the receptor structure, would it be possible to
overlap the three ligands? I think it would be very useful to zoom on this ligand overlap and to
present this illustration as a main figure. Comparing the docking poses of the three ligands in the
orthosteric binding pocket in a single panel would be highly informative and would strengthen
the discussion part on receptor antagonism and subtype selectivity. Since the orthosteric binding
pocket is well conserved in the vasopressin/oxytocin receptor family, the binding sites of
atosiban, balovaptan and SRX246 could be compared to that of retosiban in OTR, and those of
tolvaptan and mambaquaretin in V2R.
Reply: Thank you very much for your suggestion. We have now introduced a new main figure,
Fig. 6, to compare the binding poses of different antagonists, which include the three antagonists
in the current study as well as retosiban (OTR), tolvaptan (V2R), and mambaquaretin (V2R). We
also discussed in detail the specific interactions of these antagonists with the receptors, illustrated
in the newly made Supplementary Fig. 13. The corresponding text has been added as a
dedicated section (lines 466-488) in the Result section, as well as in the Discussion section
(Lines 568-586).
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
[...]
Reply: Thank you very much for your comment. The engineering of V1aR into V1aRcryo was
adopted from a previous structural study of OTR (PMID: 32832646). In the previous study, eight
mutations/truncations as well as fusion proteins were required to obtain the crystals, and the
structure provides very valuable insights into the mechanism of OTR antagonism by retosiban. In
our study, we aimed to preserve the wild-type sequence as closely as possible and significantly
reduced the equivalent mutations from 8 to 2. The two adopted mutations used previously in
OTR, S341C and N344K, were found to be essential for obtaining a stable sample suitable for
structural studies; without them, V1aR remained refractory to high-resolution structure
determination.
In the previous report (Logan, Richard Thomas (2013). The structure and function of the
vasopressin V1a receptor. University of Birmingham. Ph.D. Table 4.3), the N344K mutation of
V1aR was found not to be able to induce downstream signaling. We also used an NFAT-driven
luciferase assay to assess the G-protein signaling of V1aRcryo and found it to be signaling-
incompetent (Please see figure below).
However, V1aRcryo retains high sensitivity to antagonists atosiban, balovaptan, and SRX246
(Please see “reply to comment 3” below), validating its structural integrity. Since the current
study is focused on the molecular mechanism of antagonism, we deemed this engineering
necessary and reasonable. To better inform the readers of the properties of V1aRcryo, we
updated the text in (Lines 125-140).
2. For the radioligand binding assay, the saturation binding curve for 3H-AVP binding to
V1aRcryo (Supplementary Fig. 2a) does not reach a plateau and appears nearly linear across the
concentration range tested. This calls into question the reliability of the reported Kd values and
suggests that AVP binding is severely compromised (not slightly compromised). Accurate Kd
determination under equilibrium conditions is essential for subsequent pharmacological analyses.
It is commended to include more data points in the 3H-AVP saturation binding assay.
Reply: Thank you very much for your suggestion. To improve the accuracy of the Kd
measurement of AVP for V1aRcryo, we included more data points using higher concentrations of
3H-AVP (Supplementary Fig. 2a). The updated binding curve now reaches a plateau, and the
new Kd value is ~19nM, compared with ~13nM in the previous version of the manuscript. The
Kd value for V1aRcryo is updated in Table 3. In light of this change, we updated the description
of AVP binding from “slightly compromised” to “modestly compromised” to better reflect the
magnitude of the change and provide readers with a better understanding of the property of
V1aRcryo.
We updated Supplementary Fig. 2a, Table 3, and modified the text (line 136) to accommodate
the new changes.
3. The competition binding assays for the antagonists are also highly problematic. The authors
show that all three antagonists exhibit similar IC50s (higher IC50 for balovaptan) for V1aRcryo
compared to wtV1aR, and state that “Notably, the binding of antagonists atosiban, balovaptan,
and SRX246 to V1aRcryo, which are the focus of the current study, were almost unaltered” (line
109). However, according to basic pharmacological principles, if AVP binding is compromised
(i.e., increased Kd), and the IC50 values for antagonists are unchanged, it implies that the Kd
values for the antagonists must also be compromised to the same extent. The authors should
calculate and report the Kd values of all three antagonists using the Cheng-Prusoff equation.
Reply: Thank you for your comments, and we apologize for this issue. Based on the updated Kd
value for AVP, we converted the IC50 values for antagonists into Ki using the Cheng-Prusoff
equation. These values are now reported in the revised Supplementary Table 3. In light of this
change, we updated the statement of antagonists binding from “almost unaltered” to “V1aRcryo
remains highly sensitive to antagonists atosiban, balovaptan, and SRX246, enabling investigation
of their molecular mechanisms, which are the focus of the current study.”.
We updated Supplementary Table 3, and modified the text (lines 138-140) to accommodate
the new changes.
4. This issue also applies to the mutagenesis studies. In the mutagenesis studies, comparisons of
IC50 values across V1aR mutants are presented without confirming whether AVP binding is
preserved in each mutant. This is a critical oversight, as changes in AVP affinity would influence
competition binding results. The proper approach is to first determine AVP Kd for each mutant
and then calculate the corresponding antagonist Kd values to allow meaningful interpretation.
Reply: Thank you for your comments, and we apologize for this oversight. To address this
concern, we determined the Kd value of AVP for each mutant using the ligand-binding assays
(Supplementary Fig. 9, Table 3) and confirmed that the AVP binding for each mutant is
preserved, with no substantial changes compared to wild-type V1aR. Then, we converted the
previous IC50 values into Ki using the Cheng-Prusoff equation (Supplementary Table 3). All
previous interpretations of the data remain the same.
We made a new Supplementary Fig. 9 and modified the Supplementary Table 3 to
accommodate the changes.
5. The observed dimer interface is structurally interesting, but its physiological significance
remains uncertain. Class A GPCR dimerization is still a controversial topic. It has been well
established that class A GPCRs do form clusters or loose oligomers under physiological
conditions. However, whether they form stable dimers and how the oligomerization of class A
GPCRs affect their signaling is still elusive. The authors should consider whether the observed
dimerization may result from cryo-EM sample preparation artifacts such as the nanobody or the
receptor modifications. In this regard, functional validation, such as ligand binding or signaling
assays for dimer interface mutants like K52A and A59Y, is essential to demonstrate the relevance
of dimerization to receptor function.
Moreover, it is important to report whether monomeric particles or highly oligomerized particles
were also observed in the cryo-EM analysis. Please reference the recent study reporting higher-
order oligomeric structures of a class A GPCR (doi.org/10.1038/s41594-024-01397-1). This
would help clarify whether V1aR forms obligatory dimers, as seen in class C GPCRs, or if
dimerization represents just one of several possible oligomeric states.
Reply: Thank you very much for the suggestion. We are not the first to report the existence of
V1aR dimers in the AVP/OT family. There has been a substantial amount of evidence showing
the dimer formation among the AVP/OT family (PMID: 12554793) and their roles in beta-
arrestin association and trafficking (PMID: 14757828), and this has guided the design of
symmetric antagonists (PMID: 27420737). All of these underscore the physiological significance
of the dimer and its importance for pharmacology. Our current study provides the structural
insights into the dimer formation.
Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we used the NFAT-driven luciferase assay to assess the G-
protein signaling of wild-type V1aR and the K52A/A59Y mutant. The EC50 for AVP is 5-fold
higher for the K52A/A59Y mutant than for wild-type, and the IC50 values for all tested
antagonists are higher for the mutant as well (Supplementary Figure 7, Table 4), which
suggests that the dimer is physiologically relevant.
We did observe a small population of particles with a smaller diameter in raw images, likely
corresponding to the monomeric species. However, due to their small size and low abundance,
these particles were very likely lost during subsequent data processing and do not generate a
reliable 3D reconstruction. In contrast, no clear trimeric or tetrameric particles were detected in
our cryo-EM datasets, unlike CXCR4, for which recent cryo-EM studies have visualized trimeric
and tetrameric assemblies. Now, we reported those findings in the text and referenced the paper
of CXCR4 as well.
We made a new Supplementary Fig. 7, Table 4, and modified the text (lines 192-197, lines 247-
249) to accommodate the new changes.
6. Previous studies have reported dimeric or oligomeric structures of other class A GPCRs,
including the apelin receptor (Nat Struct Mol Biol 2022; Nat Commun 2024) and CXCR4 (Nat
Commun 2023; Cell Rep 2025). Comparing the V1aR dimer interface with these receptors would
help contextualize the findings and clarify whether this dimerization mode is unique or shared.
Reply: Thank you very much for your suggestion. We now compared the dimer interface of
V1aR with that of β1AR, rhodopsin, CXCR4, GPR3, and APJR and illustrated the comparison in
the newly made Supplementary Fig. 8 and contextualized our findings. The corresponding text
has been added in the Result section (lines 250-256).
Other minor issues
7. It would be highly informative to discuss ligand selectivity in more details, as it is an
important issue for developing antagonists for the AVP and OT receptor family. Atosiban is
commonly used as a OXTR antagonist.
Reply: Thank you very much for your suggestion. We have now discussed the selectivity in more
detail in the Discussion section (lines 568-586) and made a new Supplementary Fig. 13 to make
it more informative. Atosiban’s dual antagonism is noted and discussed.
8. Since structures of V2R-AVP and OXTR-OT are available, it would be informative to model
the binding of AVP and OT to V1aR and discuss its preference for the vasopressin and oxytocin
peptides.
Reply: Thank you for your suggestion. We generated OT-bound V1aR and AVP-bound V1aR
using Modeller based on V2R-AVP and OTR-OT structures (Supplementary Fig. 11). Using the
computationally generated models, we discussed the residues that might contribute to the
preference of AVP over OT. Phe³ of AVP inserts more deeply into the TM5–TM6 hydrophobic
cleft than Ile³ of oxytocin, enhancing hydrophobic interactions with V1aR. Moreover, Met2005.43
of V1aR will clash with Ile³(oxytocin), whereas in OTR and V2R, isoleucine at this position can
accommodate Ile³(oxytocin).
We made a new Supplementary Fig. 11 and modified the text (lines 385-396) to accommodate
the new changes.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
[...]
Reply: We sincerely thank Reviewer #3 for the thoughtful evaluation of our manuscript. As an
Early Career Researcher participating in Nature Communications’ peer review training initiative,
your perspective is invaluable to the scientific community. We appreciate the rigor of your
methodological insights. Your contributions exemplify how emerging scholars enhance academic
discourse, and we commend the journal’s commitment to fostering new voices in peer review.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
[...]
Reply: Thank you for your comment. V1aR exhibits very low, or even negligible, expression in
the common cell lines available to us. We acknowledge that we did not perform absolute
quantification to directly compare protein levels in our experimental system with those in a
subset of cells from normal tissues, as this is technically very challenging. Conventionally,
GPCR dimerization is assessed using BRET assays following 24-48 hours of transfection, an
approach that has also been applied to confirm the dimer formation of AVP/OT family members
(PMID: 12554793). However, higher expression levels increase the likelihood of dimer or even
higher-order oligomer formation. Therefore, we attempted to probe the dimerization behavior of
V1aR under a much lower expression level compared with the traditional method. In our
experimental setup of the single-molecule photobleaching approach, the transfection period was
restricted to 3 hours, a substantially shorter duration, under which V1aR remained predominantly
in the dimeric state.
2) It would be helpful if the authors could confirm that the GFP-tagged constructs are still
functionally active. E.G. do cells expressing the GFP-tagged constructs respond similarly to
agonism/antagonism compared to the non-fluorescently tagged proteins?
Reply: Thank you for your suggestion. GFP-tag was changed into mStayGold-tag for better
photostability behaviors. We used the NFAT-driven luciferase assay to assess the G-protein
signaling of wild-type V1aR and the mStayGold-tagged version. In all cases, the mStayGold-
tagged construct responds similarly to agonism by AVP and antagonism by
atosiban/balovaptan/SRX246, compared to the wild-type proteins (Supplementary Fig. 7).
We made a new Supplementary Fig. 7, Table 4, and modified the text (lines 207-209) to
accommodate the new changes.
3) The authors show a representative image in Figure 2c, but do not state what the cell in the
image is expressing. Furthermore, they indicate that only spots within the yellow circles were
chosen for further analysis, but they do not state how these spots were selected or why they were
chosen instead of the many other puncta-like objects in their image. I’m also concerned that the
representative image shows many large aggregates of protein in addition to single diffraction-
limited spots. What are these large aggregate structures? Are they an oligomerization artifact due
to the tagged protein?
Reply: Thank you for these insightful questions, and we apologize for the missing information.
In the updated Fig. 2c, the cell is expressing mStayGold-tagged V1aR K52A/A59Y (previously
shown as mEGFP-tagged WT V1aR in the original figure). This information is now provided in
the legend of the updated Fig. 2c.
Using a single-molecule photobleaching assay to distinguish monomers from dimers proved to
be extremely challenging for two main reasons:
(1) Stringent requirement for low expression levels. The expression level needs to be
sufficiently low to minimize both oligomerization and overlap of individual molecules.
We anticipated that stable expression systems or even CRISPR knock-in would lead to
large aggregates, which would preclude reliable photobleaching analysis. Therefore, as
mentioned above, we restricted the transient transfection period to less than 3 hours.
During imaging, we manually inspected the fluorescence intensity of individual cells and
selected those with relatively low fluorescence signals to reduce the probability of
overlapping molecules. However, even under these conditions, expression levels still
varied between cells within the same sample. Moreover, within a single cell, protein
density was not uniform across the entire plasma membrane. Consequently, even in low-
expression cells, many fluorescent spots likely correspond to large protein aggregates,
which is a common caveat of transient transfection; these spots were excluded from
further analysis.
(2) Photobleaching during cell screening reduces the apparent dimer fraction. As
described above, we needed to manually inspect cells to identify those with suitably low
expression levels, which were relatively rare. During this inspection, photobleaching
inevitably occurred. This process preferentially reduces the number of detectable dimeric
events: once one fluorophore in a dimer bleaches, the remaining signal becomes
indistinguishable from that of a monomer. In contrast, the number of monomeric events is
largely unaffected, because spots that are fully photobleached are simply not selected for
analysis. This concern motivated our switch from mEGFP to mStayGold, the most
photostable fluorescent protein available to date. Although the photostability of
mStayGold is significantly compromised after fixation, this change allowed us to obtain
more data of sufficient quality for statistical analysis. Nevertheless, the fraction of
dimeric events observed in our study is still likely underestimated.
Overall, the puncta-like objects that were excluded from analysis most likely represent protein
aggregates caused by transient transfection. However, they are not artifacts of the tagging using
mStayGold, as we have confirmed that the mStayGold-tagged constructs retain normal function.
Furthermore, we have additional evidence supporting that WT V1aR predominantly exists in a
dimeric state as observed in the cryo-EM structures. The dimeric assembly was functionally
validated using an NFAT-driven luciferase assay to assess the G-protein signaling of wild-type
V1aR and the K52A/A59Y mutant. The EC50 for AVP is 5-fold higher for the K52A/A59Y
mutant than for wild-type, and the IC50 values for all tested antagonists are higher for the mutant
as well (Supplementary Fig. 7, Table 4), which suggests that the observed dimer is
physiologically relevant.
4) There are no error bars on Figure 2 e or f, nor do the authors provide information about the
sample size (number of spots, number of cells, nor number biological replicates). Are these plots
from just a single ROI in a single cell each?
Reply: Thank you for the great question. After switching from mEGFP to mStayGold, we were
able to obtain more data of sufficient quality for statistical analysis (300-400 events in total). In
the updated Fig. 2e and 2f, the data are presented as mean ± SEM. For each group, the data were
obtained from three cells across two independent experiments. This information has been
included in the legend of Fig. 2 and in the Supplementary Information.
5) At least in my experience, it is very unusual to have single molecule photobleaching defined
by only monomers or dimers and not have any higher-order oligomerization states (even if only
at a small percentage). Were these curves discarded from the analysis?
Reply: Thank you for the great question. We did observe a small fraction of spots that exhibited
more than two photobleaching steps in their fluorescence intensity profiles (less than 10% of all
inspected spots). However, as mentioned above, transient transfection inevitably led to non-
uniform protein expression and overlapping molecules. Consequently, we could not reliably
determine whether spots with more than two steps represented genuine higher-order oligomeric
events, overlapping molecules, or simply protein aggregates. Because there is currently no
evidence that WT V1aR forms higher-order oligomers beyond dimers, we chose to exclude all
spots that exhibited more than two photobleaching steps from our analysis.
We have now explicitly mentioned this point in the Supplementary Information.
“Disputed spots, including those showing more than two photobleaching steps or lacking clear,
well-defined transitions in their intensity profiles, were excluded from further analysis.”
6) There is no information in the methods about how the number of bleaching steps for each
trajectory was determined. Was this just done manually from the traces or did the authors utilize
some objective criteria or algorithm?
Reply: Thank you for your comment. Because we were unable to identify a reliable algorithm
for automatic analysis, we manually inspected the fluorescence intensity profiles to determine
the number of photobleaching steps. We have now added a detailed description of how the
number of bleaching steps was determined in the Supplementary Information under “Single-
molecule photobleaching assay”.
“Raw image stacks comprising 3,000 frames were acquired at a frame rate of 5 Hz. Two
researchers independently selected approximately 100 non-overlapping, single-spot regions from
each stack using ImageJ software. The summed fluorescence intensity within a 3×3-pixel region
of interest (ROI), centered on each spot, was computed. Fluorescence intensity profiles across
the entire stack were then plotted to identify photobleaching steps for individual spots. One
researcher manually classified the bleaching curve types, and a second researcher performed an
independent review. Disputed spots, including those showing more than two photobleaching
steps or lacking clear, well-defined transitions in their intensity profiles, were excluded from
further analysis. The number of spots exhibiting distinct bleaching steps was quantified for each
experimental group and subjected to statistical analysis. Each group included three replicates
derived from two independent experiments.”

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The revised version of the manuscript by Zhong P et al. describes the cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) three-dimensional (3D) structure of the apo state of the human vasopressin V1a receptor (V1aR) and those of the receptor in complex with three different types of antagonists. These are the first high-resolution structures of V1aR ever described. Interestingly, all structures presented in this manuscript are those of homodimeric V1aR particles. In addition, the authors show that the apo state structure of V1aR displays a flat extracellular loop 2 (ECL2) including an alpha helix, a significant difference in conformation with that of the antagonist-bound receptor states (in which this ECL2 exhibits a typical antiparallel beta-sheet). This study provides a comprehensive understanding of V1aR assembly and opens the way to structure-guided development of new antagonists for treating central nervous system disorders. It also gives information about antagonist receptor selectivity.
All the criticisms and comments I raised previously were adequately addressed in the revised version. Also, the remarks from the other reviewers were addressed (to my personal point of view).
My main criticism was focused on the ligand free state of the V1aR, for which the density map of the ECL2 was missing. Due to this absence, the previous results were not in agreement with the conclusions. Thanks to the authors who collected more cryo-EM images and describe now a conformation of the ECL2 which supports their conclusions. Indeed, the number of particles was increased, the overall resolution of the cryo-EM map was improved, and more importantly the majority of ECL2 was reliably modeled. This improvement allowed the authors to show that ECL2 adopts an alpha-helical conformation in the apo state and inserts into the ligand-binding pocket. These new data are now discussed, particularly about the transition from alpha-helical (apo state) to beta-sheet (ligand-bound) conformations upon ligand binding. New figures or new panels were also added to accomodate these changes.
Among the minor comments, since the orthosteric binding pocket is well conserved in the vasopressin/oxytocin receptor family, I also asked for a comparison between the binding sites of atosiban, balovaptan and SRX246 in the V1aR with those of retosiban in the OTR and those of tolvaptan and mambaquaretin in the V2R. The authors now introduced a new main figure and a new Supplementary figure, as well as text in the Result and Discussion sections.
All other minor criticisms were addressed adequately. And consequently, text and/or illustrations were added to the revised version.
I still have one remark about reference 39. Either it is incomplete, or it is wrong. Please complete or correct.
Providing this last modification (reference 39), I consider the manuscript is now acceptable for publication in Nature Communications.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The authors have addressed most of my concerns with additional pharmacological assays, and the new data look fine. I have only one remaining minor concern. The authors note that the two introduced mutations disrupt the signaling capacity of V1aR, although ligand binding is largely unaffected. In many GPCR structural studies that used engineered receptors with impaired signaling, the structural insights typically focused on ligand binding. In this case, the discussion of the potential dimer interface should be more cautious. It would be helpful to include a brief discussion of this limitation in the manuscript.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The authors have generally addressed my comments by more clearly detailing the methods used for their selection of which cells and photobleaching spots to quantify, by more clearly describing their quantification procedure, and by verifying that the mStayGold-tagged proteins are functional. I do find their logic in describing the origin of and for excluding the quantification of large aggregates to be a bit circular.
For example, the authors claim in the rebuttal that "stable expression systems or even CRISPR knock-in would lead to large aggregates, which would preclude reliable photobleaching analysis". Yet, they also state that "Overall, the puncta-like objects that were excluded from analysis most likely represent protein aggregates caused by transient transfection." So, if I understand the argument correctly, the authors anticipate that both endogenous expression (at native protein levels) and transient over expression lead to aggregates?
However, they exclude any large spots or traces with more than 2 photobleaching steps from further analysis, "Because there is currently no evidence that WT V1aR forms higher-order oligomers beyond dimers". I find this argument very confusing.
However, the authors do clearly state in the revised methods that they select only spots that show dimer or monomer photobleaching curves and discard any traces with more than 2 photobleaching steps. Given that this is a relatively minor part of the manuscript, I feel that this is probably sufficient.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Arginine vasopressin (AVP) and oxytocin (OT) are peptide hormones critical for various physiological processes. Vasopressin receptor 1A (V1aR), a primary AVP target, is promising for central nervous system (CNS) disorder therapies, yet the mechanisms of antagonism and oligomerization remain poorly understood. Here, we present structures of human V1aR in its apo state and in complexes with antagonists: atosiban, balovaptan, and SRX246. Structural analyses reveal a dimeric V1aR assembly, validated by functional assays and imaging in cells. The apo structure shows a flat extracellular loop 2 (ECL2) with unpaired cysteines, undergoing significant conformational changes upon ligand binding. Antagonist-bound structures, combined with mutagenesis and radioligand binding assays, uncover distinct binding modes and key determinants for antagonism and selectivity. These findings provide a comprehensive understanding of V1aR assembly and dynamic regulation, offering valuable insights for structure-guided development of new antagonists targeting dimeric V1aR for CNS disorders.

## Introduction

Arginine vasopressin (AVP) and oxytocin (OT) are structurally homologous neuropeptides that regulate a variety of physiological processes through the AVP/OT receptor family: oxytocin receptor (OTR) and three vasopressin receptors (V1aR, V1bR, V2R)1–3. Among these, the vasopressin V1a receptor (V1aR), encoded by AVPR1A, is notable for its broad tissue distribution in both peripheral tissues and the central nervous system (CNS)2,4,5. Mechanistically, V1aR primarily couples with Gq/11 proteins, activating calcium-dependent signaling and protein kinase C (PKC) pathways6–8. These signaling pathways support the canonical roles of V1aR in cardiovascular and renal homeostasis, while also modulating higher-order CNS functions, including social behavior9–11, emotional reactivity12, stress adaptation13,14, and circadian timing15–17. Emerging evidence has implicated the dysregulation of V1aR signaling in several neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD)18–20, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)21,22, and Huntington’s disease (HD)23,24. This highlights V1aR as a promising therapeutic target for CNS disorders.

In line with its clinical relevance, several V1aR antagonists have progressed to various stages of therapeutic development5. Atosiban, a cyclic peptide derivative with dual inhibitory properties for AVP and OT, is approved and commonly used in Europe for the treatment of preterm labor25. Additional antagonists, such as conivaptan (a dual V1aR and V2R antagonist), have been developed for the treatment of hyponatremia26. Furthermore, CNS-penetrant V1aR-selective antagonists, including balovaptan for autism spectrum disorder (ASD)27, and SRX246 for Huntington’s disease (HD)28, have demonstrated preliminary efficacy in early-phase clinical trials. Despite these promising pharmacological profiles, the molecular mechanisms governing antagonist binding and receptor subtype selectivity remain poorly understood. This knowledge gap is largely attributed to the absence of high-resolution structural data for V1aR and its complexes with various antagonists, which hinders the optimization of V1aR-specific drug candidates.

Several structures of AVP/OT receptor family members have been resolved recently, most of which represent active-state and inactive-state conformations of V2R and OTR29–36. These structures have provided valuable insights into the ligand-binding and receptor-activation mechanisms. However, no structural information is currently available for V1aR. Notably, all currently resolved structures of V2R and OTR depict monomeric receptor states, whereas substantial evidence suggests that AVP/OT receptor family members can form homo- or heterodimers, which play important roles in downstream signaling and trafficking37,38. These findings highlight the need for further structural investigations to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying receptor dimerization.

In this work, we present the high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of human V1aR in its apo state and in complexes with three clinically relevant antagonists: atosiban, balovaptan, and SRX246. Our structural and cell-based analyses reveal the mechanistic details of V1aR homodimerization. Furthermore, the V1aR apo structure uncovers a “flat” extracellular loop 2 (ECL2) with unpaired cysteines, which undergoes significant conformational changes upon ligand binding. Comparisons among the three antagonist-bound structures highlight the key molecular determinants influencing ligand binding, receptor antagonism, and subtype selectivity. The functional significance of these residues is validated through site-directed mutagenesis and radioligand binding assays. Collectively, our findings provide a comprehensive mechanistic framework for understanding V1aR regulation and offer valuable insights for guiding drug development efforts targeting the dimeric V1aR in CNS disorders.

## Results

The overall structure of human V1aR
To obtain the structure of human V1aR, we constructed an expression vector containing full-length wild-type human V1aR with a signal peptide followed by a FLAG tag at its N-terminus. However, the protein aggregated heavily upon purification using anti-FLAG resin under various detergent conditions. To improve the biochemical behaviors of the proteins, we truncated part of the unstructured N-terminus of V1aR and introduced two mutations, S341C and N344K, which are a subset of the eight mutations used previously to stabilize OTR29 for structural studies. The resulting construct, named V1aR_cryo, was purified to homogeneity using Lauryl Maltose Neopentyl Glycol (LMNG) and Cholesteryl hemisuccinate (CHS) as detergents. V1aR_cryo in its apo state eluted as a monodisperse peak on size-exclusion chromatography (Supplementary Fig. 1a), which made it a suitable construct for cryo-EM analysis. The SDS-PAGE gel showed two bands, which likely correspond to the monomeric and the SDS-resistant dimeric species.

To evaluate the functionality of the construct, we performed cell-based ligand-binding assays to compare the ligand-binding properties of V1aR_cryo with those of the wild-type receptor. V1aR_cryo expressed at a similar level to the wild-type protein (Supplementary Fig. 2c). Although the N344K mutation renders V1aR signaling-incompetent39, ligand binding property is mostly preserved. AVP binding to V1aR_cryo was modestly compromised, similar to the effects of equivalent mutations on OT binding to OTR29 (Supplementary Fig. 2a and Supplementary Table 3). Notably, V1aR_cryo remains highly sensitive to antagonists atosiban, balovaptan, and SRX246, enabling investigation of their molecular mechanisms, which are the focus of the current study (Supplementary Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 3).

Next, we prepared V1aR_cryo in its apo form (V1aR_apo) and complex with atosiban (V1aR_atosiban), balovaptan (V1aR_balovaptan), and SRX246 (V1aR_SRX246) for cryo-EM analysis (Supplementary Fig. 1a, c–e). The initial map of V1aR_cryo was of very limited resolution (data not shown), probably due to a lack of sufficiently large features outside the micelle for accurate particle alignment. To address this problem, we performed in vitro nanobody screening (details are provided in Supplementary Information) and obtained one hit Nb1 after extensive validations (Supplementary Table 2). Nanobody Nb1 was able to form complexes with V1aR_cryo in its apo as well as ligand-bound states (Supplementary Fig. 1b–e).

We then subjected these four samples to single-particle cryo-EM analysis and determined high-resolution structures at an overall resolution of 2.6-3.0 Å assessed by the gold standard of Fourier shell correlation (FSC) = 0.143 (Fig. 1, Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4, and Supplementary Table 1). The high-quality maps for all four structures allow for reliable model building of the majority parts of V1aR, including all transmembrane (TM) regions as well as extracellular loops (ECLs). Decent local densities also facilitated accurate docking of ligands and placement of cholesterol molecules, as well as the assignment of water molecules in the structure of V1aR_SRX246 (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 5). The flexible N-terminal and C-terminal region of V1aR and some cytosolic loops between TMs such as intracellular loop 2 (ICL2) were not modeled due to maps not resolved very well in those regions. Although Nb1 was not resolved well in the final high-resolution reconstructions, the 6 Å low-pass-filtered map reveals extra densities adjacent to the cytosolic face of V1aR that closely match the shape of Nb1 (Supplementary Fig. 5e), indicating that Nb1 engages a conformationally heterogeneous epitope on the intracellular side of the receptor. We therefore infer that Nb1 serves as a fiducial mask sufficient to enable early particle classifications and global low-resolution alignment. However, its flexible orientation relative to the receptor leads to partial signal averaging and eventual loss of nanobody density during high-resolution refinement.

The dimer architecture
Previous studies have demonstrated that V1aR can form homodimers or heterodimers with related receptors such as V2R and OTR37,38. Bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET) analyses have shown that these dimeric arrangements remain stable regardless of agonist or antagonist treatment, suggesting that ligand binding does not significantly alter the dimerization state38. These insights have also facilitated the development of a dimeric agonist for OTR40. Unlike the previously reported monomeric structures of other receptors in this family, our cryo-EM structures reveal V1aR in a dimeric form, observed in both the apo state and antagonist-bound states (Fig. 1). We also observed a small population of particles with a smaller diameter in raw images, likely corresponding to the monomeric species, and tried to select these during particle picking. However, due to their small size and low abundance, these particles were lost during subsequent data processing. In contrast, no clear trimeric or tetrameric particles were detected in our cryo-EM datasets-unlike CXCR4, for which recent cryo-EM studies have visualized trimeric and tetrameric assemblies41.

The dimer interface of V1aR is quite extensive, primarily mediated by TM1, with additional contributions from the extracellular region of TM2 and the cytosolic region of TM7 (Fig. 2a). A comparison of the four structures shows that the dimers of V1aR_apo, V1aR_balovaptan, and V1aR_SRX246 share highly similar overall architectures. However, the two copies of V1aR_atosiban adopt a slightly different angle within the membrane compared to the others (Supplementary Fig. 6a), suggesting relative plasticity of the dimer interface.

To independently investigate the oligomeric state of V1aR in live cells, which has been previously reported as dimers, we employed a single-molecule photobleaching (smPB) assay, a well-established method for probing protein oligomerization42,43. In this approach, mStayGold was fused to the C-terminus of wild-type V1aR (Fig. 2b). The resulting fusion construct behaved similarly to wild-type V1aR in the NFAT-driven luciferase assay under both agonist stimulation with AVP and antagonist-mediated suppression (Supplementary Fig. 7 and Supplementary Table 4). The fusion construct was expressed at very low levels by transient transfection for a short period of time in U-2OS cells, which lack endogenous V1aR expression. Maintaining low expression levels was essential to ensure assay reliability and minimize potential dimerization artifacts caused by overexpression. Using total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy with single-molecule sensitivity, exogenously expressed V1aR-mStayGold constructs appeared as discrete fluorescent puncta on the cell surface (Fig. 2c). Continuous low-intensity laser illumination induced stepwise photobleaching of mStayGold fluorescence (Fig. 2d). For each selected punctum (Fig. 2c), the number of photobleaching steps was quantified to determine the oligomeric state of the receptor (details are described in Supplementary Information). For wild-type V1aR, approximately 75% of analyzed puncta exhibited two-step photobleaching, while the remaining 25% showed single-step bleaching (Fig. 2e). These findings are consistent with the structural observations demonstrating that V1aR forms a homodimer, and previous reports.

The detailed interactions at the dimer interface involve polar interactions on the extracellular side and hydrophobic interactions within the TM region (Fig. 2g). For polar interactions, K521.33 (numbers in superscripts correspond to Ballesteros-Weinstein numbering)44,45 form hydrogen bonds with E481.29 on the opposing protomer, a configuration that is nearly identical in V1aR_balovaptan and V1aR_SRX246, but slightly altered in V1aR_atosiban concerning bond angles. In V1aR_apo, K521.33 forms hydrogen bonds with the backbone carbonyl oxygens of D1122.64 and I1132.65 from the other receptor copy, while also interacting with Y1152.67 from the other copy via a cation-π interaction. The hydrophobic interactions are formed by Cβ-Cβ, Cβ-CA, or Cβ-O side-chain contacts through a network of small hydrophobic residues A561.37/A591.40/V601.41/A631.44 across all four structures, with an additional contribution from V641.45 in V1aR_atosiban. Similar dimer interfaces, stabilized by residues with small side chains, have been observed in the dimer of Ste2, a class D GPCR46,47. To further validate our structural models, we introduced mutations at key interface residues. Specifically, K521.33 was mutated to alanine, and A591.40 was replaced with tyrosine, a residue with a bulky side chain. These mutations resulted in a mutant V1aR that predominantly exhibits a monomeric state on the cell surface (Fig. 2f). In the NFAT-driven luciferase assay, these mutations resulted in a higher EC50 value for AVP and higher IC50 values for all antagonists tested, which suggest that the dimer assembly is physiologically relevant (Supplementary Fig. 7 and Supplementary Table 4).

A comparative survey of reported class A GPCR homodimers further contextualizes the V1aR interface. The β1-adrenergic receptor (β1AR) and rhodopsin adopt a V1aR-like arrangement with a TM1-centered interface, whereas the principal contact surface is on TM5-TM6 in CXCR4, on TM5–TM6 in GPR3, and within ECL1 between TM2 and TM3 in APJR (Supplementary Fig. 8)48–56. Except for APJR, whose dimerization relies mainly on ECL1 contacts, these dimers including V1aR are stabilized predominantly by extended hydrophobic interactions within the TM region.

The ligand-free state
ECL2 in GPCRs is well-known for its length variation and structural diversity, playing crucial roles in receptor signaling57–59. Our structures reveal that ECL2 of V1aR adopts distinct configurations in the apo state compared to the antagonist-bound states (Fig. 3a), whereas the ECL2 conformations in the antagonist-bound states are very similar (Supplementary Fig. 6b). In the antagonist-bound states, ECL2 adopts an “up” conformation, forming an antiparallel β-sheet fold that projects away from the binding pocket at an approximately perpendicular orientation relative to the membrane (Fig. 3a). This “up” conformation of ECL2 creates a large, solvent-exposed cavity capable of accommodating ligands. In the apo state, the majority of ECL2 was modeled reliably, supported by well-defined local densities (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 6c). Notably, two segments that form the antiparallel β-sheet fold observed in the antagonist-bound states adopt alpha-helical conformation in the apo structure: one becomes a continuation of TM4, while the other inserts into the ligand-binding pocket (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 6c). The remainder of ECL2 (residues 193–201, sequence between the two beta-sheet segments) is visible as continuous density in the 6 Å low-pass-filtered map (Supplementary Fig. 5f), but could not be confidently modeled. Given the relatively planar orientation of ECL2 relative to the membrane in the apo structure, we designate this arrangement the “flat” conformation.

These extensive conformational changes in ECL2 are also accompanied by significant structural rearrangements in ECL1, the extracellular loop connecting TM2 and TM3 (Fig. 3a). One notable outcome of the conformational changes of ECL2 is their impact on the conserved disulfide bond between ECL2 and TM3, a hallmark feature of class A GPCRs57,60. In the antagonist-bound structures of V1aR, C203 in ECL2 forms a disulfide bond with C1243.25 in TM3. Interestingly, in the apo state, this canonical disulfide bond is not formed, with C203ECL2 and C1243.25 remaining unpaired (Fig. 3c). The cryoEM densities for both unpaired cysteines are well resolved and supported by clear density for surrounding residues (Fig. 3b).

Mechanistically, the inserted part of ECL2 in the apo structure is stabilized in the “flat” configuration through a combination of hydrophobic interactions and hydrogen bonds with residues from TM2, TM3, TM4, TM5, and TM6 (Fig. 3d). Specifically, W204ECL2 inserts into a hydrophobic pocket created by P1072.59, W1112.63, and K1283.29, while W2115.34 inserts into a separate hydrophobic pocket composed of Y2165.39, V2175.40, and M2205.43 on TM5, and F3076.51 on TM6. Additionally, stabilizing hydrogen bonds are observed between R118ECL1 and the carbonyl oxygen of D202ECL2, Q1082.60, and the backbone nitrogen of A205ECL2, K1283.29 and the carbonyl oxygen of W204ECL2, together with the side chain of Q209ECL2, Q1854.61 and the carbonyl oxygen of I208ECL2 (Fig. 3d). Collectively, these interactions anchor ECL2 within the binding pocket in the apo state. This inserted ECL2 with unpaired cysteines was also observed in the recently reported GPR4 structure61.

The antagonistic mechanism of atosiban
The cryo-EM structure of the V1aR_atosiban complex reveals that atosiban spans the entire ligand-binding pocket of V1aR. The high-quality density map enables precise modeling of various parts of the ligand (Fig. 4a). As an OTR/V1aR dual antagonist62,63, atosiban retains the nine-residue peptide backbone of oxytocin, the endogenous OTR agonist, including the conserved disulfide-bridged ring. However, it incorporates modifications at four key positions to confer proteolytic resistance and enhance pharmacokinetic properties: Cys1 is replaced with mercaptopropionic acid (Mpa), eliminating the free amino group; Tyr2 is replaced by D-Tyr(Et), a D-enantiomer bearing an ethoxy moiety; Gln4 is substituted with Thr; and Leu8 is replaced with Orn (Fig. 4e)64. In the cryo-EM structure, atosiban adopts a similar overall conformation to oxytocin (Fig. 4e) and engages V1aR through a highly coordinated network of polar and hydrophobic interactions that collectively stabilize the receptor in an inactive conformation (Fig. 4b). Mpa1 of atosiban forms a disulfide bond with Cys6 of atosiban, reinforcing the rigidity of the cyclic ring, and establishes a hydrogen bond with Q3116.55 of V1aR via its terminal carboxyl group. D-Tyr(Et)2 of atosiban inserts into a polar sub-pocket formed by TM1, TM2, and TM7, engaging Q1042.56 and S3387.42 through its ethoxy oxygen, while its terminal carboxyl group interacts with K1283.29 and Q1854.61 of V1aR (Fig. 4c). Notably, K1283.29 and Q1854.61 are essential residues for AVP recognition35. Due to their functional importance, mutations at these sites significantly impair [3H]AVP binding, making them unsuitable for use in competition assays involving atosiban, balovaptan, and SRX246. Mutational analyses highlight the important role of S3387.42, as mutations of this residue result in a 24-fold reduction in Ki (Fig. 4d, Supplementary Figs. 9 and 10a, and Supplementary Table 3). Other residues also contribute to ligand stabilization. Ile3 of atosiban is embedded in a hydrophobic pocket formed by TM3, TM5, and TM6, contacting M1353.36, Y2165.39, V2175.40, M2205.43, and F3086.52 of V1aR (Fig. 4c). Mutagenesis of these positions (V217A, M220I, F308A) significantly reduces atosiban binding, highlighting the functional importance of this hydrophobic cleft (Fig. 4d). Thr4 of atosiban forms a stabilizing hydrogen bond with Q3116.55 of V1aR, while Asn5 of atosiban contributes to ligand recognition via a hydrogen bond with backbone oxygen of A205ECL2 and amino-π stacking with W204ECL2 of V1aR. The linear tail of atosiban—comprising Pro7, Orn8, and Gly9—extends towards the extracellular vestibule. Orn8 further stabilizes the ligand by forming hydrogen bonds with E541.35 and T3317.35 of V1aR, reinforcing the anchorage of the C-terminal segment.

In the absence of the V1aR-AVP complex for direct comparison, we compared the structures of V1aR–atosiban and OTR–oxytocin complexes (PDB: 7RYC)33 to gain deeper insights into ligand recognition and receptor antagonism. The ligand-binding poses in the two complexes exhibit a high degree of overlap (Fig. 4f). However, distinct ligand binding results in noticeable differences between the two receptors, particularly in the extracellular portion of TM1, the intracellular portions of TM5, as well as TM6 and TM7 (Fig. 4g). A key difference lies in the remodeling of TM7. In the OTR–oxytocin complex, Tyr2 of oxytocin forms a critical hydrogen bond with the carbonyl oxygen of L3167.39 and induces a bend in TM7 near A3187.41, promoting rearrangement of W2886.48 on TM6 and activating the CWxP toggle switch, a key structural hallmark of GPCR activation65–68. In contrast, the substitution of Tyr2 with D-Tyr(Et) in atosiban eliminates the phenolic hydroxyl group, in the meantime, the additional ethyl group on D-Tyr(Et)2 enhances local hydrophobicity and shape complementarity, which collectively help maintaining TM7 in its canonical α-helical form, thus stabilize the receptor in its inactive state (Fig. 4h). Meanwhile, in the structure of OTR–oxytocin complex, F2846.44, a key residue within the conserved PXF motif of class A GPCRs, undergoes an outward movement induced by the aforementioned conformational rearrangement of W2886.48, thereby promoting OTR activation. In contrast, in the V1aR–atosiban complex, W3046.48 retains its canonical inactive conformation, preventing the conformational transition of Y3006.44 (the equivalent of F in the PXF motif) that is required for V1aR activation (Fig. 4j).

Additionally, in the V1aR-atosiban structure, an ionic lock involving R1493.50, D1483.49 in DRY motif69, and T2896.33 stabilizes TM6 in an inward conformation, preventing the formation of the G protein–binding cavity. In contrast, in the active OTR–oxytocin complex, this ionic lock is disrupted: R1373.50 disengages from D1363.49 and instead stacks with Y243 of the miniGq/i, thereby stabilizing the active conformation (Fig. 4k). Consequently, in the V1aR-atosiban structure, the cytoplasmic end of TM6 fail to undergo the outward displacement required for G protein engagement, rendering the intracellular cavity inaccessible to the α5 helix of Gαq. The tail of atosiban (Pro7, Orn8, and Gly9) also contributes to the inactivation of V1aR. Previous studies have revealed the important roles of Mg2+ in the activation of both OTR and V1aR29,33. In the V1aR-atosiban structure, the binding of the atosiban tail positions Orn8 very close to where Mg2+ is located in the OTR–oxytocin structure. This, combined with the altered local structure, results in the exclusion of Mg2+ (Fig. 4i).

Besides the OTR–oxytocin active-state structure, V2R–AVP signaling complexes have also been resolved and provide family-level templates for comparison. Consistent with pharmacological profiles, V1aR binds AVP with markedly higher affinity than oxytocin70. To gain insights into this difference, we computationally generated active-state models of V1aR–AVP and V1aR–oxytocin using MODELLER71,72, followed by restrained docking, guided by the OTR–oxytocin and V2R–AVP structures (Supplementary Fig. 11)32,33,72. Because AVP and oxytocin differ only at positions 3 and 8 (AVP: Phe3/Arg8; oxytocin: Ile3/Leu8), our models attribute the selectivity to two cooperative features: (i) Phe3 (AVP) inserts more deeply into the TM5–TM6 hydrophobic cleft than Ile3 (oxytocin), enhancing hydrophobic interactions. Moreover, Met2005.43 of V1aR will clash with Ile3 (oxytocin), whereas in OTR and V2R, isoleucine at this position can accommodate Ile3 (oxytocin). (ii) Arg8 (AVP) forms electrostatic contacts with residues in TM1, stabilizing the rim interactions.

Together, these features elucidate the molecular mechanism by which atosiban stabilizes V1aR in an inactive state, effectively preventing G protein engagement and downstream signaling.

Binding modes of balovaptan and SRX246
In addition to the peptide-based antagonist atosiban, we accurately resolved the binding modes of two representative V1aR-specific small-molecule antagonists: balovaptan and SRX2465. Both small molecules antagonize the V1aR receptor by inducing a conformation change very similar to that caused by atosiban (Supplementary Fig. 6b). While both occupy the orthosteric pocket (Fig. 5a, b), balovaptan and SRX246 exhibit distinct chemotypes and binding modes.

Balovaptan is a non-peptidic small-molecule V1aR antagonist, originally developed by Roche for the treatment of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), aiming to modulate AVP-mediated social cognition pathways27. Balovaptan features a rigid tricyclic core composed of a [1,4]-benzodiazepine fused with a [1,2,4]-triazole ring. This core scaffold is further decorated with a methyl group at position 5 and a chlorine substituent at position 8, which enhance the hydrophobic character of the molecule (Fig. 5c). These hydrophobic features enable balovaptan to deeply insert into the ligand-binding pocket of V1aR (Fig. 5a), which is lined by V1323.33, M1353.36, Y2165.39, V2175.40, M2205.43, F3076.51, and F3086.52 (Fig. 5d). Mutagenesis of key residues within this pocket impairs ligand binding to varying degrees, with V217A showing the most significant effect, underscoring the essential role of this residue in stabilizing the molecule (Fig. 5g, Supplementary Figs. 9, 10b, and Supplementary Table 3). Additionally, the triazole nitrogen atoms form polar contacts with K1283.29 and Q1854.61, further stabilizing the core scaffold within the pocket. Extending from its tricyclic core, balovaptan possesses a flexible cyclohexyl–ether–pyridyl side chain that projects towards the polar sub-pocket formed by TM1, TM2, and TM7. The ether oxygen forms a hydrogen bond with Q1042.56, while the pyridine nitrogen engages in a polar network involving S3387.42 and Q1042.56 (Fig. 5d). These interactions are further supported by mutational data (Fig. 5g). Notably, mutation of A3347.38 on TM7 to methionine—the equivalent residue found in V1bR, V2R, and OTR—introduces a potential steric clash with the pyridyl ring, resulting in a decrease in binding affinity (Fig. 5g). This observation indicates the importance of steric compatibility at the pocket entrance for optimal ligand accommodation and partially explains the receptor subtype specificity for balovaptan.

SRX246, developed by Azevan Pharmaceuticals, is another non-peptidic V1aR antagonist currently under clinical investigation for the treatment of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)73 and other affective disorders, such as HD28,74, which are linked to AVP signaling. Unlike balovaptan, SRX246 employs a structurally modular strategy centered on a rigid β-lactam (azetidinone) core, flanked by four discrete functional regions (Zones A–D)75,76 that engage distinct subpockets within the receptor through fragment-like interactions (Fig. 5b, e). Zone A consists of an oxazolidin-2-one linked to a terminal phenyl ring. The aromatic moiety is buried within a hydrophobic subpocket formed by F1894.65, F207ECL2, and Y2165.39, while the carbonyl group of the oxazolidinone engages in water-mediated hydrogen bonds with K1283.29 and Q1854.61. K1283.29 also forms a hydrogen bond with the carbonyl group of the azetidinone core directly (Fig. 5f). Zone B contains a styrenyl-like π-conjugated system co-planar with the β-lactam ring, reinforcing molecular rigidity and π–π interaction potential. The terminal phenyl ring inserts into the same but deeper hydrophobic cleft between TM3 and TM6, forming extensive contacts with M1353.36, V2175.40, M2205.43, F3076.51, and F3086.52 (Fig. 5f). Functional mutagenesis further validates the structural dependency of Zone B, as mutations such as V217A, M220I, and F307Y significantly reduce binding affinity (Fig. 5h, Supplementary Figs. 9 and 10c, and Supplementary Table 3). Notably, the equivalent residue of M2205.43 in V2R and OTR is isoleucine, which partially explains the receptor subtype specificity of SRX246. Zone C consists of a phenylethyl group linked to the central amide nitrogen. The phenylethyl group is attached via an amide linkage, with its phenyl ring forming a polar interaction with Q1042.56. Meanwhile, the carbonyl oxygen of the amide engages in a hydrogen bond with K1283.29. Zone D extends into the extracellular vestibule through a bipiperidine group that forms a polar interaction with E541.35 and engages in hydrophobic interaction with A511.32 (Fig. 5f), further stabilizing the distal portion of the molecule and contributing to the overall rigidity of the ligand–receptor complex.

Collectively, SRX246 exemplifies a fragment-based multivalent design, featuring a rigid central core paired with adaptable peripheral regions to achieve comprehensive engagement of the orthosteric site. In contrast, balovaptan employs a single deep-binding hydrophobic core, complemented by a flexible polar extension that interacts with the extracellular face of the receptor. In both antagonist-bound structures, Mg2+ was not observed due to the disruption of the Mg2+ binding site. Despite their contrasting structural architectures, both ligands stabilize V1aR in a conformation that is incompatible with G protein engagement, underscoring distinct yet convergent strategies for receptor antagonism.

Comparison of AVP/OT family-antagonist interactions
We first observed that SRX246 exhibits a modular architecture, with distinct chemical moieties occupying spatially separable regions of the V1aR binding pocket. Leveraging this feature, we used SRX246 as a reference scaffold to compare antagonist binding modes across receptors in the AVP/OT family29,35. For clarity, substructures extending into zones A and D were collectively assigned to the “upper pocket”. The “upper pocket” comprises the extracellular-facing portion of the orthosteric cleft, including the interface with the extracellular loops (ECLs). In contrast, moieties corresponding to zones B and C were assigned to the “bottom pocket” that is the deeper transmembrane cavity (Fig. 6a).

We then aligned available antagonist–receptor complex structures to the V1aR–SRX246 complex to compare ligand binding poses. This analysis revealed that AVP/OT-family antagonists can be broadly grouped into three classes based on their penetration depth and extent of pocket engagement. Class I is represented by atosiban, a macrocyclic nonapeptide antagonist that, like SRX246, spans nearly the full width and depth of the orthosteric site—engaging both the upper and bottom pockets. It further extends toward the pocket mouth of the binding pocket to make auxiliary contacts with polar residues on TM1. Class II is exemplified by mambaquaretin-1 (MQ1), a compact, toxin–like mini-protein antagonist. In contrast to SRX246, MQ1 primarily occupies the upper pocket and forms extensive contacts with the ECLs, with limited insertion into the deeper transmembrane cavity. Class III consists of small-molecule antagonists such as retosiban, balovaptan, and tolvaptan. These ligands are enriched in hydrophobic and heteroaromatic ring systems and preferentially occupy the bottom pocket. Unlike peptide- or protein-like antagonists, these compounds make limited contact with the ECLs and instead exploit the hydrophobic subcavity at the base of the orthosteric site.
