### Reviewer 2

This paper presents the first high-resolution cryo-EM structures of the human V1aR in its apo state and in complex with three
clinically relevant antagonists, atosiban, balovaptan, and SRX246. A major finding is the dimeric assembly of V1aR, which
contrasts with previously resolved monomeric structures of related receptors and most of other class A GPCRs, providing
crucial insights validated by cell-based assays. The study also elucidates significant conformational changes in ECL2, which
transitions from a "flat" conformation in the apo state to an "up" conformation upon antagonist binding, creating a
ligand-accommodating cavity. Furthermore, the structures and associated functional assays detail the distinct binding modes
of the antagonists and identify key molecular determinants governing V1aR antagonism and subtype selectivity. This
comprehensive mechanistic framework for V1aR regulation and assembly offers invaluable insights, paving the way for
structure-guided design of novel antagonists.
However, while the structural data are of high quality and the reported V1aR dimer interface is intriguing, several major
concerns regarding receptor function and pharmacology studies significantly limit the mechanistic impact and physiological
relevance of the findings.
1. The only assay used to characterize the engineered V1aR as V1aRcryo is the 3H-AVP radioligand binding assay. This
does not assess whether the receptor is functionally competent. It is critical to perform signaling assays such as Ca2+
mobilization or G protein coupling to demonstrate that the engineered receptor retains signaling capacity. Without such data,
it is unclear whether the receptor represents a physiologically relevant signaling-competent conformation.
2. For the radioligand binding assay, the saturation binding curve for 3H-AVP binding to V1aRcryo (Supplementary Fig. 2a)
does not reach a plateau and appears nearly linear across the concentration range tested. This calls into question the
reliability of the reported Kd values and suggests that AVP binding is severely compromised (not slightly compromised).
Accurate Kd determination under equilibrium conditions is essential for subsequent pharmacological analyses. It is
commended to include more data points in the 3H-AVP saturation binding assay.
3. The competition binding assays for the antagonists are also highly problematic. The authors show that all three
antagonists exhibit similar IC50s (higher IC50 for balovaptan) for V1aRcryo compared to wtV1aR, and state that “Notably,
the binding of antagonists atosiban, balovaptan, and SRX246 to V1aRcryo, which are the focus of the current study, were
almost unaltered” (line 109). However, according to basic pharmacological principles, if AVP binding is compromised (i.e.,
increased Kd), and the IC50 values for antagonists are unchanged, it implies that the Kd values for the antagonists must also
be compromised to the same extent. The authors should calculate and report the Kd values of all three antagonists using the
Cheng-Prusoff equation.
4. This issue also applies to the mutagenesis studies. In the mutagenesis studies, comparisons of IC50 values across V1aR
mutants are presented without confirming whether AVP binding is preserved in each mutant. This is a critical oversight, as
changes in AVP affinity would influence competition binding results. The proper approach is to first determine AVP Kd for
each mutant and then calculate the corresponding antagonist Kd values to allow meaningful interpretation.
5. The observed dimer interface is structurally interesting, but its physiological significance remains uncertain. Class A
GPCR dimerization is still a controversial topic. It has been well established that class A GPCRs do form clusters or loose
oligomers under physiological conditions. However, whether they form stable dimers and how the oligomerization of class A
GPCRs affect their signaling is still elusive. The authors should consider whether the observed dimerization may result from
cryo-EM sample preparation artifacts such as the nanobody or the receptor modifications. In this regard, functional
validation, such as ligand binding or signaling assays for dimer interface mutants like K52A and A59Y, is essential to
demonstrate the relevance of dimerization to receptor function.
Moreover, it is important to report whether monomeric particles or highly oligomerized particles were also observed in the
cryo-EM analysis. Please reference the recent study reporting higher-order oligomeric structures of a class A GPCR
(doi.org/10.1038/s41594-024-01397-1). This would help clarify whether V1aR forms obligatory dimers, as seen in class C
GPCRs, or if dimerization represents just one of several possible oligomeric states.
6. Previous studies have reported dimeric or oligomeric structures of other class A GPCRs, including the
apelin receptor (Nat Struct Mol Biol 2022; Nat Commun 2024) and CXCR4 (Nat Commun 2023; Cell Rep 2025). Comparing
the V1aR dimer interface with these receptors would help contextualize the findings and clarify whether this dimerization mode
is unique or shared.
Other minor issues
7. It would be highly informative to discuss ligand selectivity in more details, as it is an important issue for developing
antagonists for the AVP and OT receptor family. Atosiban is commonly used as a OXTR antagonist.
8. Since structures of V2R-AVP and OXTR-OT are available, it would be informative to model the binding of AVP and OT to
V1aR and discuss its preference for the vasopressin and oxytocin peptides.

Reply: Thank you for these insightful questions, and we apologize for the missing information.
In the updated Fig. 2c, the cell is expressing mStayGold-tagged V1aR K52A/A59Y (previously
shown as mEGFP-tagged WT V1aR in the original figure). This information is now provided in
the legend of the updated Fig. 2c.
Using a single-molecule photobleaching assay to distinguish monomers from dimers proved to
be extremely challenging for two main reasons:
(1) Stringent requirement for low expression levels. The expression level needs to be
sufficiently low to minimize both oligomerization and overlap of individual molecules.
We anticipated that stable expression systems or even CRISPR knock-in would lead to
large aggregates, which would preclude reliable photobleaching analysis. Therefore, as
mentioned above, we restricted the transient transfection period to less than 3 hours.
During imaging, we manually inspected the fluorescence intensity of individual cells and
selected those with relatively low fluorescence signals to reduce the probability of
overlapping molecules. However, even under these conditions, expression levels still
varied between cells within the same sample. Moreover, within a single cell, protein
density was not uniform across the entire plasma membrane. Consequently, even in low-
expression cells, many fluorescent spots likely correspond to large protein aggregates,
which is a common caveat of transient transfection; these spots were excluded from
further analysis.
(2) Photobleaching during cell screening reduces the apparent dimer fraction. As
described above, we needed to manually inspect cells to identify those with suitably low
expression levels, which were relatively rare. During this inspection, photobleaching
inevitably occurred. This process preferentially reduces the number of detectable dimeric
events: once one fluorophore in a dimer bleaches, the remaining signal becomes
indistinguishable from that of a monomer. In contrast, the number of monomeric events is
largely unaffected, because spots that are fully photobleached are simply not selected for
analysis. This concern motivated our switch from mEGFP to mStayGold, the most
photostable fluorescent protein available to date. Although the photostability of
mStayGold is significantly compromised after fixation, this change allowed us to obtain
more data of sufficient quality for statistical analysis. Nevertheless, the fraction of
dimeric events observed in our study is still likely underestimated.
Overall, the puncta-like objects that were excluded from analysis most likely represent protein
aggregates caused by transient transfection. However, they are not artifacts of the tagging using
mStayGold, as we have confirmed that the mStayGold-tagged constructs retain normal function.
Furthermore, we have additional evidence supporting that WT V1aR predominantly exists in a
dimeric state as observed in the cryo-EM structures. The dimeric assembly was functionally
validated using an NFAT-driven luciferase assay to assess the G-protein signaling of wild-type
V1aR and the K52A/A59Y mutant. The EC50 for AVP is 5-fold higher for the K52A/A59Y
mutant than for wild-type, and the IC50 values for all tested antagonists are higher for the mutant
as well (Supplementary Fig. 7, Table 4), which suggests that the observed dimer is
physiologically relevant.

more than two photobleaching steps in their fluorescence intensity profiles (less than 10% of all
inspected spots). However, as mentioned above, transient transfection inevitably led to non-
uniform protein expression and overlapping molecules. Consequently, we could not reliably
determine whether spots with more than two steps represented genuine higher-order oligomeric
events, overlapping molecules, or simply protein aggregates. Because there is currently no
evidence that WT V1aR forms higher-order oligomers beyond dimers, we chose to exclude all
spots that exhibited more than two photobleaching steps from our analysis.
We have now explicitly mentioned this point in the Supplementary Information.
“Disputed spots, including those showing more than two photobleaching steps or lacking clear,
well-defined transitions in their intensity profiles, were excluded from further analysis.”
6) There is no information in the methods about how the number of bleaching steps for each
trajectory was determined. Was this just done manually from the traces or did the authors utilize
some objective criteria or algorithm?
Reply: Thank you for your comment. Because we were unable to identify a reliable algorithm
for automatic analysis, we manually inspected the fluorescence intensity profiles to determine
the number of photobleaching steps. We have now added a detailed description of how the
number of bleaching steps was determined in the Supplementary Information under “Single-
molecule photobleaching assay”.
“Raw image stacks comprising 3,000 frames were acquired at a frame rate of 5 Hz. Two
researchers independently selected approximately 100 non-overlapping, single-spot regions from
each stack using ImageJ software. The summed fluorescence intensity within a 3×3-pixel region
of interest (ROI), centered on each spot, was computed. Fluorescence intensity profiles across
the entire stack were then plotted to identify photobleaching steps for individual spots. One
researcher manually classified the bleaching curve types, and a second researcher performed an
independent review. Disputed spots, including those showing more than two photobleaching
steps or lacking clear, well-defined transitions in their intensity profiles, were excluded from
further analysis. The number of spots exhibiting distinct bleaching steps was quantified for each
experimental group and subjected to statistical analysis. Each group included three replicates
derived from two independent experiments.”
